---
title: The p-Zassenhaus filtration
kind: definition
summary: 'The $p$-Zassenhaus filtration $G_{(n)}$ of a profinite group is the fastest descending series with $[G_{(i)},G_{(j)}]\subseteq G_{(i+j)}$ and $G_{(i)}^p\subseteq G_{(ip)}$. Jennings: $G_{(n)}=G\cap(1+I^n)$ in $\mathbb F_p[[G]]$. In $U_n(\mathbb F_p)$ it is the superdiagonal filtration.'
tags: [pro-p-groups, galois-cohomology, group-theory]
---

**Definition.** Let $p$ be a prime and $G$ a profinite group. For closed subgroups $H,K$ of $G$, let $[H,K]$ be the closed subgroup generated by the commutators $[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$ with $x\in H$ and $y\in K$, and let $H^p$ be the closed subgroup generated by the $p$th powers of elements of $H$. The *$p$-Zassenhaus filtration* of $G$ is defined by

$$G_{(1)}=G,\qquad G_{(n)}=G_{(\lceil n/p\rceil)}^p\prod_{i+j=n}[G_{(i)},G_{(j)}]\quad(n\ge2)$$

[@minactan2015kernel, §2, p. 4] [@minacrogelstadtan2015dimensions, §1, p. 1]. Equivalently, it is the fastest descending series of closed subgroups starting at $G$ such that

$$[G_{(i)},G_{(j)}]\subseteq G_{(i+j)},\qquad G_{(i)}^p\subseteq G_{(ip)}\qquad(i,j\ge1)$$

[@efrat2014zassenhaus, §1, p. 1] [@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, Definition 3.1 and (3.2), p. 7]. Its terms are also called the dimension subgroups in characteristic $p$ [@minacrogelstadtan2015dimensions, §1, p. 1]. Efrat writes $G_n$ for $G_{(n)}$.

By these inclusions each $G_{(n)}/G_{(n+1)}$ is central in $G/G_{(n+1)}$ and is an elementary abelian $p$-group. The first terms are $G_{(2)}=G^p[G,G]$ and

$$G_{(3)}=G^p[G,[G,G]]\quad(p\ne2),\qquad G_{(3)}=G^4[G,G]^2[G,[G,G]]\quad(p=2)$$

[@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, p. 7]. If $G$ is a finitely generated pro-$p$ group, then $H^1(G,\mathbb F_p)\cong(G/G_{(2)})^*$ [@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, (4.2), p. 9], and every $c_n(G)=\dim_{\mathbb F_p}G_{(n)}/G_{(n+1)}$ is finite [@minacrogelstadtan2015dimensions, §1, p. 1].

**Basic properties.** These are proved here. Items 1 and 2 go by induction on $n$ from the recursive definition, in which the indices $\lceil n/p\rceil$, $i$ and $j$ used to build $G_{(n)}$ are all smaller than $n$.

1. *Functoriality.* If $f:G\to H$ is a continuous homomorphism, then $f(G_{(n)})\subseteq H_{(n)}$, with equality if $f$ is surjective. So each $G_{(n)}$ is a closed characteristic subgroup, $H_{(n)}\subseteq G_{(n)}$ for every closed subgroup $H\subseteq G$, and $(G_1\times G_2)_{(n)}=(G_1)_{(n)}\times(G_2)_{(n)}$. The last equality is also noted in [@minacrogelstadtan2015dimensions, Remark 2.3, p. 4].

   *Proof.* By induction the $G_{(k)}$ with $k<n$ are normal, so the factors in the definition of $G_{(n)}$ are closed normal subgroups. Their product is compact, hence closed, so $G_{(n)}$ is the closed subgroup generated by the set $X_n$ of $p$th powers of elements of $G_{(\lceil n/p\rceil)}$ and commutators $[x,y]$ with $x\in G_{(i)}$, $y\in G_{(j)}$, $i+j=n$. By continuity $f$ maps the closed subgroup generated by a set into the closed subgroup generated by its image. If $f$ is onto, the image of the first is compact, hence closed, and contains the image of the set, so the two subgroups agree. By induction $f(X_n)$ lies in the corresponding set for $H$, and equals it if $f$ is onto. Applying this to automorphisms, to inclusions, and to the projections and inclusions of the factors of $G_1\times G_2$ gives the rest. $\square$

2. *Lower central series and powers.* With $\gamma_1(G)=G$ and $\gamma_{k+1}(G)=[\gamma_k(G),G]$, we have $\gamma_n(G)\subseteq G_{(n)}$. If $n\le p^h$, then $y^{p^h}\in G_{(n)}$ for every $y\in G$.

   *Proof.* For $n\ge2$, $\gamma_{n}(G)=[\gamma_{n-1}(G),G]\subseteq[G_{(n-1)},G_{(1)}]\subseteq G_{(n)}$. For the powers, induct on $h$; the case $h=0$ is $n=1$. If $h\ge1$, then $\lceil n/p\rceil\le p^{h-1}$, so $y^{p^{h-1}}\in G_{(\lceil n/p\rceil)}$ by induction, and its $p$th power lies in $G_{(n)}$. $\square$

3. *Unitriangular groups.* Let $\mathbb F$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$ and $U_n(\mathbb F)$ the group of upper unitriangular $n\times n$ matrices over $\mathbb F$. Let $N_k$ be the space of matrices $(a_{ij})$ with $a_{ij}=0$ unless $j-i\ge k$, and $\Gamma_k=1+N_k$. Then $U_n(\mathbb F)_{(k)}=\Gamma_k$ for every $k\ge1$. In particular $U_n(\mathbb F_p)_{(n)}=1$, as Mináč and Tân state [@minactan2015kernel, Lemma 2.4, p. 5], and with item 1 every continuous homomorphism $G\to U_n(\mathbb F)$ kills $G_{(n)}$; for $\mathbb F=\mathbb F_p$ see [@minactan2015kernel, Lemma 2.5(b), p. 6]. More precisely, if $\rho:G\to U_{m+1}(\mathbb F)$ is continuous and $g\in G_{(m)}$, then $\rho(g)-1$ is supported on the corner entry $(1,m+1)$, and $g\mapsto\rho(g)_{1,m+1}$ is a homomorphism $G_{(m)}\to\mathbb F$.

   *Proof.* Write $U=U_n(\mathbb F)$. Since $N_kN_l\subseteq N_{k+l}$ and $N_n=0$, each $\Gamma_k$ is a subgroup, with $(1+a)^{-1}=\sum_{r\ge0}(-a)^r$, and $\Gamma_n=1$. For $a\in N_i$ and $b\in N_j$,

   $$(1+a)^p=1+a^p\in\Gamma_{pi},\qquad [1+a,1+b]=1+(1+a)^{-1}(1+b)^{-1}(ab-ba)\in\Gamma_{i+j},$$

   the first because $p$ divides $\binom pr$ for $0<r<p$, the second by expanding $(1+a)(1+b)-(1+b)(1+a)$. So the descending series $(\Gamma_k)$ satisfies the two inclusions of the second description. As $U_{(1)}=\Gamma_1$, induction on $k$ gives, for $k\ge2$,
   $$U_{(k)}\subseteq\Gamma_{\lceil k/p\rceil}^p\prod_{i+j=k}[\Gamma_i,\Gamma_j]\subseteq\Gamma_{p\lceil k/p\rceil}\Gamma_k=\Gamma_k.$$
   Conversely, for $i<j$ and $t\in\mathbb F$ put $E_{ij}(t)=1+te_{ij}$, where $e_{ij}$ is the matrix unit. If $j-i\ge2$, the commutator formula gives $E_{ij}(t)=[E_{i,i+1}(1),E_{i+1,j}(t)]$, since $e_{i,i+1}e_{i+1,j}=e_{ij}$ while $e_{i+1,j}e_{i,i+1}$, $e_{i,i+1}e_{ij}$ and $e_{i+1,j}e_{ij}$ are $0$. By induction on $j-i$, $E_{ij}(t)\in[U_{(1)},U_{(j-i-1)}]\subseteq U_{(j-i)}$. Finally, $\Gamma_k$ is generated by the $E_{ij}(t)$ with $j-i\ge k$. Indeed, for $a,b\in N_k$ we have $(1+a)(1+b)\equiv1+a+b$ modulo $N_{2k}\subseteq N_{k+1}$, so $1+a\mapsto a+N_{k+1}$ is an isomorphism $\Gamma_k/\Gamma_{k+1}\to N_k/N_{k+1}$. Hence for $1+a\in\Gamma_k$, the product $h$ of the $E_{ij}(a_{ij})$ with $j-i=k$, in any order, satisfies $h^{-1}(1+a)\in\Gamma_{k+1}$, and descending induction on $k$, starting from $\Gamma_n=1$, proves the claim. So $\Gamma_k\subseteq U_{(k)}$. For the last assertion, $\rho(G_{(m)})\subseteq U_{m+1}(\mathbb F)_{(m)}=\Gamma_m=1+\mathbb Fe_{1,m+1}$ by item 1, and $(1+se_{1,m+1})(1+ue_{1,m+1})=1+(s+u)e_{1,m+1}$. $\square$

4. *Separation.* If $G$ is pro-$p$, then $\bigcap_nG_{(n)}=1$. If moreover $G$ is finitely generated, each $G_{(n)}$ is open, so the $G_{(n)}$ form a base of open neighbourhoods of $1$.

   *Proof.* Let $V$ be an open normal subgroup of $G$, so that $P=G/V$ is a finite $p$-group. A finite $p$-group acting linearly on a nonzero finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_p$-vector space fixes a nonzero vector, because its nontrivial orbits have length divisible by $p$. By induction on the dimension, $P$ acts on $\mathbb F_p[P]$ by left multiplication through upper unitriangular matrices in a suitable basis, which gives an injective homomorphism $P\to U_N(\mathbb F_p)$ with $N=|P|$. By items 1 and 3, $P_{(N)}=1$, and item 1 for the surjection $G\to P$ gives $G_{(N)}\subseteq V$. The open normal subgroups of a profinite group intersect in $1$. If $G$ is finitely generated, then $G/G_{(n)}$ has order $p^{c_1(G)+\cdots+c_{n-1}(G)}$, which is finite, so $G_{(n)}$ is a closed subgroup of finite index, hence open. $\square$

**Jennings' theorem.** Let $I$ be the augmentation ideal of the completed group algebra $\mathbb F_p[[G]]$, the closed ideal generated by the elements $g-1$ with $g\in G$. For every profinite group $G$,

$$G_{(n)}=G\cap(1+I^n)\qquad(n\ge1).$$

For finite $G$ this is a theorem of Jennings and Brauer, and an inverse limit argument extends it to profinite groups [@efrat2014zassenhaus, §6, p. 9]. For a free pro-$p$ group $S$ on $x_1,\ldots,x_d$, the Magnus isomorphism $\mathbb F_p[[S]]\cong\mathbb F_p\langle\langle X_1,\ldots,X_d\rangle\rangle$, $x_i\mapsto1+X_i$, makes this explicit: $S_{(n)}$ consists of the $s\in S$ such that $s-1$ has no terms of degree below $n$ [@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, (3.3) and the display after it, p. 8] [@minactan2015kernel, Lemma 2.2(c), p. 5]. For $s\in S_{(n)}\setminus S_{(n+1)}$ the degree-$n$ part of $s-1$ is the *initial form* of $s$, and this identifies $S_{(n)}/S_{(n+1)}$ with a space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $n$ [@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, Definition 3.2 and the paragraph before it, p. 8].

**Graded objects.** Let $G$ be a finitely generated pro-$p$ group. The graded space $\mathfrak L(G)=\bigoplus_{n\ge1}G_{(n)}/G_{(n+1)}$, with bracket induced by commutators and $p$-map induced by $p$th powers, is a restricted Lie algebra over $\mathbb F_p$ [@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, §3.2, p. 8]. For $g\in G_{(n)}\setminus G_{(n+1)}$, the assignment $gG_{(n+1)}\mapsto(g-1)+I^{n+1}$ induces a monomorphism of restricted Lie algebras from $\mathfrak L(G)$ to the graded algebra of the augmentation filtration of the group algebra, which makes that graded algebra the restricted universal enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak L(G)$ [@minacpasiniquadrellitan2022mild, Proposition 3.4, p. 9]. For the completed algebra, $\mathrm{gr}\,\mathbb F_p[[G]]=\bigoplus_{n\ge0}I^n/I^{n+1}$ is the restricted universal enveloping algebra of $\mathfrak L(G)$, and its Hilbert series is

$$\sum_{n\ge0}\dim_{\mathbb F_p}(I^n/I^{n+1})\,t^n=\prod_{n\ge1}\Bigl(\frac{1-t^{np}}{1-t^n}\Bigr)^{c_n(G)}$$

[@minacrogelstadtan2015dimensions, Theorem 2.1, p. 4]. This series is $1/(1-dt)$ for a free pro-$p$ group of rank $d$, $1/(1-t)^d$ for $\mathbb Z_p^d$, and $1/(1-dt+t^2)$ for a [Demushkin group](demushkin-group.md) of rank $d$ [@minacrogelstadtan2015dimensions, Examples 2.4 (1), (4) and (6), p. 5].

**Example: $\mathbb Z_p$.** This is checked here. As $\mathbb Z_p$ is abelian, $(\mathbb Z_p)_{(n)}=(\mathbb Z_p)_{(\lceil n/p\rceil)}^p$ for $n\ge2$. Since $p^{h'}\ge\lceil n/p\rceil$ exactly when $p^{h'+1}\ge n$, induction gives $(\mathbb Z_p)_{(n)}=p^h\mathbb Z_p$, with $h$ the least integer such that $p^h\ge n$. So $c_n(\mathbb Z_p)$ is $1$ if $n$ is a power of $p$ and $0$ otherwise, and the product above telescopes to $1/(1-t)$, as the case $d=1$ requires. The filtration differs from the descending $p$-central series, $G^{(1)}=G$ and $G^{(n+1)}=(G^{(n)})^p[G^{(n)},G]$ [@minactan2015kernel, §2, p. 4], for which $\mathbb Z_p^{(n)}=p^{n-1}\mathbb Z_p$.

**Where it appears.**

- *Unipotent representations.* The [kernel-unipotent conjecture](kernel-unipotent-conjecture.md) predicts that for $G=G_F(p)$, with $F$ containing a primitive $p$th root of unity, $G_{(n)}$ is the intersection of the kernels of all continuous homomorphisms $G\to U_n(\mathbb F_p)$. Item 3 gives one inclusion for every profinite $G$. For free pro-$p$ groups equality holds for every $n$ [@minactan2015kernel, Theorem 2.6(a), p. 7] [@efrat2014zassenhaus, Theorem A, p. 2]. Efrat proves $G_{(n+1)}=\bigcap\ker(G\to U_{n+1}(\mathbb F_p))$ for $G=S/N$, with $S$ free profinite and $N\subseteq S_{(n)}$ closed and normal, under a condition on the $n$-fold Massey products of $G/G_{(n)}$ [@efrat2014zassenhaus, Theorem A$'$ and the paragraph before it, p. 2]. The knowledgebase's proofs of the conjecture for [Demushkin groups](kernel-unipotent-property-for-demushkin-groups.md) and [free products](kernel-unipotent-property-for-free-products-of-demushkin-and-free-groups.md) read the initial form of $g\in G_{(m)}\setminus G_{(m+1)}$ off the corner entries of item 3, through Jennings' theorem.
- *Mod-$\ell$ abelian-by-central quotients.* For a prime $\ell$ and a pro-$\ell$ group $G$, the quotients $G^a$ and $G^c$ of [abelian-by-central Galois groups](abelian-by-central-galois-group.md) are $G/G_{(2)}$ and $G/G_{(3)}$ for the $\ell$-Zassenhaus filtration. Indeed $G_{(2)}=G^\ell[G,G]$, and since $[x,y]^{-1}=[y,x]$, $[G_{(1)},G_{(2)}]=[G_{(2)},G_{(1)}]$. So $G_{(3)}=G^\ell[G,G_{(2)}]$ for odd $\ell$, where $\lceil3/\ell\rceil=1$, and $G_{(3)}=G_{(2)}^2[G,G_{(2)}]$ for $\ell=2$. These are the subgroups $G^{(2)}$ and $G^{(3)}$ defined there.
- *Koszulity.* [Mild pro-$p$ groups](mild-pro-p-groups-and-koszul-duality.md) are defined through this filtration; when such a group has quadratic cohomology, that cohomology is quadratically dual to its graded group algebra. In the [minimal Galois cohomology quotient](minimal-galois-cohomology-quotient.md), the subgroup $K_p(G)$ is $G_{(3)}$.
